1	# AI assistants (MCP setup)
2	
3	DataQ ships a built-in [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server so AI assistants — Claude Desktop, Claude.ai, VS Code / GitHub Copilot, Cursor — can answer questions like *"what failed today?"* or *"run the orders suite"* against your live DataQ instance, with the same per-suite permissions as the signed-in user.

5	## Endpoint & authentication
6	
7	The server is mounted on the deployed app at:
8	
9	```text
10	https://<your-dataq-host>/mcp/
11	```
12	
13	!!! warning "Keep the trailing slash"
14	    `/mcp` answers with a **307 redirect** to `/mcp/`, and some HTTP clients drop the
15	    `Authorization` header when following redirects — which then surfaces as a
16	    confusing 401. Always configure clients with the `/mcp/` form.
17	
18	The endpoint accepts the **same credentials as the REST API** (ADR [0008](adr/0008-mcp-server.md) / [0026](adr/0026-auth-api-keys-and-principal-seam.md)): an OIDC bearer token (Azure AD or Cognito), or a **DataQ API key** (`dq_live_…`). Without auth configured, the endpoint is only mounted in local dev-bypass mode — never unauthenticated in a deployed environment.
19	
20	!!! info "Email-OTP deployments: MCP works, with an API key"
21	    A deployment running **email one-time codes instead of SSO** (ADR
22	    [0032](adr/0032-email-otp-signin.md)) has no identity provider to issue bearer
23	    tokens, so an **API key is the only `/mcp` credential** there — mint one as
24	    below and use it exactly the same way. Everything else is identical, including
25	    all 48 tools and per-suite permissions. Two rejections are deliberate in that
26	    mode: a raw JWT is refused (there is nothing to validate it against), and your
27	    **sign-in session is never accepted** — it is a browser credential and does not
28	    authenticate `/mcp`, whether presented as a bearer or carried as a cookie.

30	### Getting a token

32	**Recommended — a DataQ API key (PAT):** mint one via `POST /api/v1/me/api-keys`

161	### Checks
162	
163	| Tool | What it answers |
164	|---|---|
165	| `list_checks` | "What does the orders suite actually check?" — every check's config, kind, dimension |
166	| `get_check` | "What is this check actually asserting?" — one check's full definition |
167	| `get_check_history` | "Has the row-count check been flaky?" — recent *result* history for one check; for how its definition changed, use `list_check_versions` |
168	| `list_check_versions` | "Who changed this threshold?" — one check's *edit* history: every snapshot's config and thresholds as they were at that version |
169	| `create_check` | "Add a null check on email" — authors a check on a suite you can edit |
170	| `update_check` | "Loosen the null check on email to warn at 2%" — a partial update; `config` replaces the whole configuration rather than merging into it |
171	| `delete_check` | "Remove the row-count check from orders" — permanently deletes a check **and every result it ever recorded, plus every incident it raised, including open ones**; prefer `snooze_check` to just stop alerting |
172	| `snooze_check` | "Stop alerting on the freshness check until tomorrow" (or, with no duration, "turn alerts back on") — mutes alerts only; the check still runs, still fails, and still opens an incident. **Suppression is per _run_**: the alert is withheld only when every failing check in that run is snoozed |
173	| `restore_check_version` | "Undo that threshold change" — puts a check back to a snapshot from `list_check_versions`; additive (nothing is renumbered or deleted), and the only path that *clears* a field back to empty |
174	| `dryrun_check` | "Would a not-null check on email pass right now?" — previews a check against live data without saving anything. Reads what a real run would read, so on flat-file / Iceberg targets it inherits the run target's sampling |

177	
178	| Tool | What it answers |
179	|---|---|
180	| `list_runs` | "Show me the recent runs" / "find the run that failed". 214	### Assets & incidents
215	
216	Assets are the grain people reason in ("is `orders` healthy?"); suites are the grain checks are
217	authored in. Incidents are the deduplicated, stateful roll-up of repeated failures.
218	
219	| Tool | What it answers |
220	|---|---|
221	| `list_assets` | "What tables do we monitor?" / "which assets are unhealthy?" — every asset with its health. The numbers are **workspace-true** (ADR [0037](adr/0037-workspace-visible-asset-identity.md)): aggregated over every composing suite, including ones the caller cannot see, so they are not "your" checks |
222	| `get_asset` | "Is the orders table healthy, and what feeds it?" — the workspace-true summary + per-dimension scorecard + the composing suites the caller may view (`restricted_suite_count` counts the rest) + the lineage neighbourhood, qualified when a lineage source is failing or stale |
223	| `list_incidents` | "What's broken right now?" — open/acknowledged/resolved incidents, scoped to suites the caller can see, so an empty result means "nothing visible to you", not "nothing is wrong". Also takes `since_hours`/`until_hours`, filtered on `last_seen_at` (most recent breach, not when first opened). Incidents auto-resolve on the first passing result, so this answers "what's unresolved now", not "what failed during period X" — a resolved failure earlier in the window won't appear even under a time filter; use `list_runs` for that question |
224	| `get_incident` | "Why did this open, and what else broke at the time?" — the evidence card snapshotted at the last occurrence; carries no failing sample rows by design |
225	| `ack_incident` | "I'm on it" — records that someone owns the incident. Changes nothing about the data and does **not** stop alerts; use `snooze_check` for that |
226	| `resolve_incident` | "The backfill fixed it" — declares the problem over. Does not re-run anything, and the next failing run opens a **new** incident |

243	| Symptom | Cause / fix |
244	|---|---|
245	| 401 on every request | Token expired (~1 h) → paste a fresh one. Or the client followed the `/mcp` → `/mcp/` redirect and dropped the header → use `/mcp/` directly. |
246	| 307 responses | Missing trailing slash — configure `/mcp/`. |
247	| Server absent / connection refused locally | The MCP server is unmounted unless the deployment has a working sign-in configuration — SSO (`AZURE_*`), email OTP (`AUTH_EMAIL_*` + an allowlist), or local dev-bypass (fail-closed by design). |
248	| 401 with an API key on an email-OTP deployment | Check you sent the **API key**, not your session cookie/token: in OTP mode a `dq_live_…` key is the only credential `/mcp` accepts. |
249	| Tool call returns "not found" for a suite you can see in the UI as someone else | MCP calls run as the token's user — suite access is per-user, same as the web app. |

def _rediss_safe_url(url: str) -> str:
    """A ``rediss://`` URL celery will accept: default ``ssl_cert_reqs=required``."""
    from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlsplit

    parts = urlsplit(url)
    if parts.scheme != "rediss" or "ssl_cert_reqs" in parse_qs(parts.query):
        return url
    separator = "&" if parts.query else "?"
    return f"{url}{separator}ssl_cert_reqs=required"

1	# Security & data handling
2	
3	How DataQ authenticates users, stores secrets, handles the data it sees, and what it keeps.
4	This is a plain-language overview for people evaluating or operating DataQ. It is **not** a
5	legal compliance certification — much of GDPR/HIPAA is organizational (DPAs, BAAs, consent,
6	lawful basis) and is the deploying organization's responsibility.
7	
8	## Authentication & access
9	
10	- **Single sign-on (OIDC).** Users sign in through your identity provider; DataQ is
11	  provider-neutral (validated against Azure AD and AWS Cognito). The backend validates the
12	  token on every request — there is no local password store.
13	- **Who may hold an account is your decision, not your IdP's.** DataQ provisions a user on
14	  first successful sign-in, so without a gate the identity provider's *registration* policy
15	  silently becomes DataQ's *access* policy. That is fine for an invite-only tenant and wrong
16	  for a provider with self-service sign-up. Two independent controls:
17	  - Keep the identity provider invite-only (the AWS reference stack sets
18	    `allow_admin_create_user_only` on the Cognito pool; an Azure AD tenant is invite-only by
19	    nature).
20	  - Set `OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS` / `OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` as the app-side allowlist. It is
21	    checked on **every request**, not only at first sign-in, so removing an entry revokes an
22	    existing account rather than merely blocking a new one.
23	
24	  Leaving the allowlist empty means "admit anyone the issuer vouches for" — deliberately, so
25	  that upgrading DataQ can never lock an existing workspace out — and the API logs
26	  `auth_oidc_no_signup_allowlist` at **WARNING** on every boot in that state. If you see that
27	  line, confirm your IdP is invite-only.
28	- **Personal access tokens (PATs).** For headless / AI-client use, users mint `dq_live_`
29	  tokens ([API keys](api-keys.md)). Tokens are **hashed (SHA-256) at rest** — the plaintext is
30	  shown once and never stored — and carry the **same authz as the user**, on REST and MCP.
31	  They can be scoped with an expiry and revoked.
32	- **Email one-time codes (OTP).** For deployments with **no identity provider**, a human can
33	  sign in by proving they own a mailbox: DataQ mails a 6-digit code, and verifying it sets an
34	  **HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax** session cookie (fixed lifetime, default 24 h, **no refresh
35	  token** — signing in again is the refresh). Logout revokes the session server-side, and both
36	  expiry and revocation are checked on every request. Sessions are hashed (SHA-256) at rest,
37	  like PATs. Sign-up is **allowlist-only** — there is no open registration. MCP does **not**
38	  accept a session: it is a browser credential, and PATs remain the headless credential
39	  (ADR [0032](adr/0032-email-otp-signin.md)).
40	  **`Secure` is inferred, not unconditional:** by default the backend reads the
41	  `X-Forwarded-Proto` the proxy forwards, and marks the cookie `Secure` only when that says
42	  `https`. That is only as trustworthy as the proxy. The reference frontend nginx forwards the
43	  **edge's** header and falls back to its own `$scheme` only on a direct connection
44	  (it used to overwrite the
45	  header with its own plaintext upstream scheme, which dropped `Secure` on live HTTPS), so
46	  inference is correct on that stack. If you front DataQ with **your own** proxy, confirm it
47	  forwards the real client-facing scheme — or simply set `AUTH_SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=true`,
48	  which any HTTPS deployment can do and which stops consulting the header at all. Leave it
49	  unset only for genuinely plain-HTTP local dev: a hard-coded `Secure` there fails *silently*
50	  (the browser accepts the `Set-Cookie` and then never sends it back).
51	  **Before turning OTP on for real users**, run the admin-gated SMTP pre-flight test — `POST
52	  /api/v1/admin/auth-email/test` sends a real message to the caller's own address over the
53	  configured `AUTH_EMAIL_*` transport and, on failure, reports exactly which stage broke
54	  (`connect` / `tls` / `auth` / `send`) rather than a generic error. It never accepts a
55	  recipient argument — it can only mail the admin who called it, and that address is echoed
56	  back in the response **by design** (it's the point of the check). The SMTP password never
57	  appears in the response or in any log line; the recipient address never appears in a log
58	  line either, only in the response, to the same admin who supplied it by calling the endpoint.
59	  **Transport options:**
60	  `AUTH_EMAIL_TLS_MODE` picks `starttls` (default) / `implicit` (SMTPS on :465) / `none`
61	  (plaintext — test-only, loudly warned on every send, and there is no way to disable that
62	  warning), and `AUTH_EMAIL_CA_BUNDLE` names a PEM the mailer trusts for a relay on a private
63	  CA. The bundle is scoped to the mailer's own connection only — it never widens or replaces
64	  the trust store any other TLS client in the process relies on (Key Vault, Snowflake, ADLS,
65	  webhooks). There is deliberately **no** option to skip certificate verification: a private
66	  CA bundle is judged to cover the legitimate case, and disabling verification was rejected as
67	  a shortcut around it rather than shipped as a convenience.
68	  It is **capped per admin** (`ADMIN_EMAIL_PREFLIGHT_PER_10MIN`, default 3 per 10 minutes),
69	  because every call is a real
70	  connection to your mail relay: admin-gating bounds *who* can open one, not *how many*, and a
71	  scripted or compromised admin token could get your sending account throttled or blocked by
72	  the relay — a worse outage than the misconfiguration the pre-flight exists to catch. Over the
73	  cap is a plain `429`; the cap fails **open** if the counter store is unavailable, and `0`
74	  disables it.
75	
76	### Email as the root of trust (read this before enabling OTP)
77	
78	Under email OTP, **the mailbox is the credential**. The consequences are not subtle, and they
79	are the reason this mode is opt-in rather than the default:
80	
81	- **Mailbox compromise is account compromise.** Anyone who can read the address's inbox can
82	  sign in as that person and see every suite they own or are shared on. There is no second
83	  factor to fall back on.
84	- **Mailbox compromise of an admin is workspace compromise.** If the address is on
85	  `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`, that access is workspace-wide — including every suite's failing-row
86	  samples, the one place PII can appear.
87	- **One user row per normalized email**, deliberately. An OTP sign-in whose address matches an
88	  existing SSO-provisioned user resolves to **that** user, so grants, shares and PATs never
89	  fragment across authenticators. The flip side: in a deployment running **both** SSO and OTP,
90	  an emailed code is an alternative route into an SSO identity. If your IdP enforces MFA and
91	  your mail does not, OTP is the weaker of the two doors — decide that deliberately, and
92	  consider keeping the allowlist to addresses that have no SSO identity.
93	- **Mitigations DataQ does apply:** codes expire in 10 minutes, are single-use, allow at most
94	  5 verification attempts, and a new request invalidates the previous code; requests are capped
95	  **per mailbox** as well as per IP; the sign-in endpoints return an identical response *body and
96	  status* whether or not an address is known, so the response content cannot be used to enumerate
97	  who has an account. The
98	  code-request endpoint also holds **every** such response to a common minimum latency
99	  (`AUTH_OTP_REQUEST_MIN_SECONDS`, default 1s), so the code-mint and mail-send round trip an
100	  eligible address incurs no longer stands out against an ineligible one's in-memory lookup.
101	  **What the floor does not cover, stated plainly:** a mail send *slower* than the floor still
102	  overruns it, so a degraded relay (bounded by `AUTH_EMAIL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, default 5s) re-opens a
103	  narrower version of the channel; a genuine SMTP failure still answers 502/503 where a working
104	  send answers `ok`, which is deliberate (a mail outage must not be a silent no-op — ADR 0032 §7);
105	  and setting the floor to `0` removes it. **Code *verification* carries the same floor on its own
106	  setting** (`AUTH_OTP_VERIFY_MIN_SECONDS`, default 0.5s):
107	  every rejected code answers an
108	  identical 401, but an address that has a live code outstanding does more database work than one
109	  that has none, so the rejection's *timing* used to reveal which — and cheaply, because a code is
110	  minted only for an *allow-listed* address, so a single request-a-code call against the address
111	  being probed (which answers identically either way, revealing nothing itself) is what sets that
112	  difference up. Every 401 is now held to the same minimum. A *successful* verification is deliberately **not** held (a caller who knows the
113	  code learns nothing from that), a database round trip slower than the floor still overruns it,
114	  and `0` removes it here too. Treat both floors as raising the attacker's cost from a handful of
115	  samples to a statistical exercise, not as a constant-time guarantee.
116	- **Mitigations that are yours:** MFA on the mailbox, a mail domain with SPF/DKIM/DMARC, and a
117	  minimal allowlist. If you have an IdP, prefer SSO — OTP exists for the case where you do not.
118	
119	- **Per-suite authorization.** Access is granted per suite (**view / edit**); a caller only
120	  ever sees suites they own or are shared on. There are no ambient "see everything" reads
121	  except the Admin role below.
122	- **Workspace roles — Admin / Member / Viewer.** A stored `users.role` (ADR 0033), not just
123	  an env allowlist. **Admin** has workspace-wide visibility over every suite, its results,
124	  and schedules, and is the *only* role that can create, edit, delete or re-auth a
125	  **connection** — a Member can reference, test and run against an existing connection but
126	  cannot mutate or re-credential it (closes the earlier hole where any authenticated user
127	  could delete or re-point the Snowflake connection every suite ran on). Testing a **saved**
128	  connection is deliberately Member+ rather than Admin-only: authoring a suite against a connection you
129	  cannot verify is not a workable flow, and a test reveals nothing a Member could not
130	  already learn by running a suite. Testing an **unsaved draft** is Admin-only, because that
131	  request carries caller-supplied config rather than config an admin stored. **Viewer** is capped at `view` everywhere, including on
132	  any share it receives, and cannot test a connection — the probe opens an outbound
133	  connection using stored credentials, which a read-only tier has no reason to trigger.
134	  The Viewer cap is enforced at the point of use, not only when a share is granted, so
135	  demoting someone to Viewer immediately downgrades any `edit` share they already hold. Because Admin visibility includes
136	  failing-row samples (the one place PII can appear), **grant it sparingly** and treat a
137	  data-access audit trail as a prerequisite before granting it in a regulated deployment.
138	  `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` still resolves to Admin as a **bootstrap / break-glass** path for a
139	  fresh or locked-out workspace — keep that allowlist minimal, and prefer in-app role
140	  management (**Admin → Users**) once at least one Admin exists. It only ever *grants*:
141	  removing an address never demotes anyone, so demotion has exactly one route, where the
142	  guard runs.
143	- **An env-level actor can always mint an Admin.** This is the deliberate cost of keeping a
144	  break-glass path, and it is worth stating rather than leaving implicit: **anyone who can set
145	  environment variables on the API container can make themselves a workspace admin**, without
146	  a role change, an audit line, or anyone's approval. Treat write-access to the API's
147	  environment as equivalent to workspace-admin when you do access reviews. In steady state,
148	  leave the allowlist empty.
149	- **You cannot remove the last Admin.** A role change must leave at least one **stored-role**
150	  admin; allowlist-resolved admins deliberately do not count toward that (the env entry can
151	  vanish on the next deploy, which would leave the workspace with no admin and no in-app way
152	  to mint one). Promote a successor first. Role changes are **audited durably**: every change
153	  writes an append-only `audit_events` row (`user.role_change`, old and new role, actor,
154	  `request_id`) **inside the same transaction as the change**, queryable by a workspace
155	  admin at `GET /api/v1/admin/audit-events` (ADR 0041) — alongside the structured log line.
156	  Every row is hash-chained to the one before it, so a direct database edit or deletion
157	  outside the app is detectable (see [Compliance](#compliance-gdpr-ccpa-cpra-hipaa)
158	  below).

160	## Network exposure
161	
162	- The **frontend is the only public surface**; the API runs on **internal ingress** and is
163	  reached only through the frontend's same-origin `/api`, `/healthz`, and `/mcp` proxy
164	  (ADR 0028 §5). All traffic is over **HTTPS/TLS**.
165	- The **MCP** AI-assistant endpoint is **fail-closed** — unauthenticated requests are rejected
166	  (ADR 0008), and it is not mounted at all unless the deployment has a working sign-in
167	  configuration. It authenticates from the `Authorization` header only and **never reads a
168	  cookie**, so a signed-in browser lured to a hostile page cannot be used to drive it.
169	  In an **OTP-only** deployment there is no identity provider, so a **PAT is the only
170	  credential MCP accepts**: a session token is rejected by prefix before any validation, and
171	  a bearer that is neither is rejected outright rather than handed to an unconfigured
172	  validator — the absence of a JWT verifier is a refusal, never a skipped check.
173	- **Browser security headers.** Every response from the frontend carries a
174	  **Content-Security-Policy** (`default-src 'self'`, `script-src 'self'`, `object-src 'none'`,
175	  `frame-ancestors 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`), **HSTS**, **X-Frame-Options**,
176	  **X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff**, **Referrer-Policy** and **Permissions-Policy**. The CSP
177	  is the backstop that matters here specifically because the UI renders values that came from
178	  *your warehouse* — failing-row samples, error text, custom SQL. `connect-src` is configured
179	  per deployment (`DATAQ_CSP_CONNECT_SRC`) because the sign-in flow talks directly to your
180	  identity provider; the shipped default (`https:`) is permissive so that upgrading the image
181	  cannot break an existing sign-in, and the reference stacks narrow it to their exact IdP
182	  origins.
183	- **Edge rate limiting (AWS).** In addition to the in-app limiter below, the CloudFront
184	  distribution carries a WAF per-IP rate ceiling. The two are not redundant: the app limiter
185	  is per-token, understands DataQ's request classes, and **fails open** if its Redis store is
186	  unavailable — so it is deliberately biased toward availability. The WAF rule sheds a flood
187	  *before* it reaches the application at all.
188	- **CSRF.** The session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`, which blocks cross-site POSTs; that only
189	  holds while every state-changing endpoint is a POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE, so the test suite
190	  audits the whole route table for a GET that mutates. Sign-in and sign-out are both POST-only,
191	  and the SPA and API share an origin through the proxy, so a cross-site request can neither
192	  carry nor read the cookie.
193	- **Two coordinated auth-mode selectors.** The frontend's runtime `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE` and the
194	  backend's inferred mode (SSO variables, or the OTP mailer + allowlist block) are separate
195	  contracts — neither can derive the other. Set them together; the full table is in
196	  the repository's `deploy/README.md` and
197	  [`.env.app.example`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/.env.app.example). The
198	  backend refuses to start on a half-configured OTP block rather than come up unable to log
199	  anybody in.

201	## Secrets
202	
203	- Datasource credentials, webhook signing keys, and channel secrets are held in a **secret
204	  store behind a seam** — Azure Key Vault in the primary reference deployment, AWS Secrets
205	  Manager on the AWS stack, OpenBao/Vault self-hosted — never in the database or in git. The
206	  app reads them via a managed identity (Azure) or the task IAM role (AWS).
207	- Secret **references** (names), not secret values, are stored alongside connections. Deleting
208	  a connection removes its secret (soft-delete on Key Vault).
209	- A reference is **server-owned**: a client may echo back the one already stored on a
210	  connection, but may never introduce or repoint one. Otherwise a caller could name someone
211	  else's secret and have the server resolve it on their behalf.
212	- **A stored credential is never sent to a destination the caller changed.** Editing a config
213	  field that decides where a credential goes — Snowflake `account`, ADLS `account_url`,
214	  S3/dbt `endpoint_url`, Unity Catalog `workspace_url`, Iceberg `catalog_uri`/`warehouse`/
215	  `properties`/`secret_property`, Airflow `base_url`, dbt `artifacts_uri` — requires re-supplying that
216	  credential in the same request, or the update is rejected (`422 credential_redirect`).
217	  Moving a connection to a new host is a supported operation; doing it with a credential you
218	  do not know is not. This is why an Admin, who may **rotate** a credential, still cannot
219	  **read** one.
220	- Inbound webhooks are authenticated: ADF by a shared secret, Airflow and dbt by an
221	  **HMAC-SHA256** signature keyed on a stored signing key.

223	## The data DataQ sees, stores, and redacts
224	
225	DataQ runs checks *against* your data; it is **not** a copy of your data. What it persists:
226	
227	- **Metadata** — suites, checks, connection config (no secrets), schedules, trigger bindings.
228	- **Results** — per-check pass/fail + a numeric `metric_value`, and for failing checks a
229	  small **failing-row sample**.
230	- **Failing-row samples are the one place results can carry PII/PHI.** They are **redacted at
231	  the boundary, column-aware**: a suite's **column policy** (auto-derived by a classifier or
232	  set by hand) keeps non-sensitive breach values debuggable while masking PII columns to
233	  `<redacted>`. The numeric counts and row/column shape are kept.
234	- **Logs & traces** are PII-redacted at the logger level, and secret values never enter them.
235	
236	## Retention
237	
238	- Failing-row **samples are purged** after a retention window (PII-minimisation), while the
239	  aggregatable **`metric_value` history is kept** for trends and baselines — so you lose the
240	  raw rows but keep the signal.

242	## Encryption
243	
244	- **In transit:** HTTPS/TLS on every public surface, and TLS to PostgreSQL (`sslmode=require`)
245	  and to the AWS cache (`rediss://`). Two internal hops are plaintext, both deliberately and
246	  both stated rather than glossed: the Azure frontend→api hop, which never leaves the
247	  Container Apps environment; and — on AWS only — the **CloudFront→ALB origin hop**, because
248	  that stack has no custom domain and therefore no certificate the load balancer could serve.
249	  The second one does cross the AWS network, so it is a real, tracked gap rather than a
250	  contained one.
251	- **At rest:** PostgreSQL, the object stores, and the secret store (Key Vault / AWS Secrets
252	  Manager) encrypt at rest in both reference deployments. The AWS cache (ElastiCache — the
253	  Celery broker and rate-limit counters, not a data store) currently does **not**.

279	### Customer-managed keys (CMK)
280	
281	Data at rest is encrypted with **service-managed keys** by default on both clouds.
282	CMK — where you hold the key — is **not wired into the IaC in this repo**, and the
283	reason splits into one product constraint and a set of deployment prerequisites.
284	
285	**The product constraint: on Azure, CMK is creation-time-only.** Microsoft is
286	explicit — *"You can select the mode only at server creation time. You can't change
287	the mode from one to another for the lifetime of the server."* The only route to
288	CMK on an existing server is restoring a backup onto a **new** one, so it is a data
289	migration rather than a Terraform toggle, and it is one-way: reverting to
290	service-managed keys requires another restore.
291	([Limitations of CMK](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/postgresql/security/security-data-encryption#limitations-of-customer-managed-keys-cmk))
292	
293	**The prerequisites, which a deployment either meets or does not:**
294	
295	- **Your IaC must own the database server from creation.** A stack that attaches to
296	  a pre-existing server has no server resource to hang a key on.
297	- **The key vault must be non-destroyable.** If the vault holding a CMK is deleted,
298	  the server goes **Inaccessible** and denies every connection — so purge protection
299	  must be on, which is irreversible once enabled. Azure additionally requires
300	  90-day deleted-vault retention, a value that *cannot be changed after the vault is
301	  created*: a vault set lower needs a new vault, not a setting change.
302	- **You must commit to key rotation operationally.** A key that expires, is
303	  disabled, or becomes unreachable takes the database offline within about an hour.
304	
305	Meeting all three is a deployment topology, not a feature flag — which is why CMK is
306	documented here rather than shipped as an option that could be enabled unsafely. A
307	stack that provisions its own server and a purge-protected vault can adopt it; the
308	maintainers' reference deployment does neither, so it is out of scope there.

310	## Column classification from your warehouse
311	
312	DataQ masks failing-row samples by default and surfaces only what it can justify
313	showing. The strongest justification available is **your own governance**:
314	if a column is classified in the warehouse, DataQ reads that classification and
315	treats it as the floor — a suite-level setting cannot lift it.
316	
317	### The convention
318	
319	A **fixed, documented convention**, not a per-connection mapping. A mapping would
320	be more flexible and worse: every deployment would express the same idea
321	differently, the mapping itself would become an unreviewed security control, and a
322	typo in it would silently un-mask a column.
323	
324	Tag your **columns** with the key **`dataq_classification`** (matched
325	case-insensitively):
326	
327	| Value | Effect |
328	|---|---|
329	| `sensitive` · `pii` · `confidential` · `restricted` · `secret` | **Always masked.** A suite policy cannot show it |
330	| `public` · `non_sensitive` · `nonsensitive` | Cleared — may be shown, unless the value itself is affirmatively personal data |
331	| anything else | **Ignored**, exactly as if untagged — see below |
332	
333	**Snowflake additionally honours its own `PRIVACY_CATEGORY`**, set by Snowflake's
334	built-in classification. Its values (`IDENTIFIER`, `QUASI_IDENTIFIER`,
335	`SENSITIVE`) all mean personal data, so all three mask. It has no clearing side:
336	Snowflake omits the tag for data it does not consider personal rather than marking
337	it public, so an unexpected value means *unknown*, not *safe*.
338	
339	**An unrecognised value is ignored rather than guessed at.** Guessing has only two
340	directions, and one of them un-masks data. `internal` is the worked example: it
341	sounds like a classification and is commonly the default stamp on everything, so
342	reading it as a clearance would clear whole tables in exactly the organisations
343	careful enough to tag them.
344	
345	**Inherited tags are not read.** A tag applied to a table or schema is reported by
346	the warehouse against every column beneath it; DataQ accepts only tags applied to
347	the **column itself**. An inherited tag is a statement about the container, and
348	reading one as a per-column clearance would clear a whole schema from a single
349	misplaced `public`.
350	
351	**The tag name is matched without its namespace**, and that is a constraint on
352	you rather than a feature: DataQ honours a tag *named* `dataq_classification`
353	wherever it lives, because knowing which database or schema should be
354	authoritative would require per-deployment configuration, and this convention is
355	deliberately fixed. **Do not create tags with this name for any other purpose** —
356	a same-named tag elsewhere carrying a `public`-family value would be honoured as
357	a clearance.
358	
359	### Who can apply the tags, and what DataQ needs to read them
360	
361	Two different privileges, and conflating them is the usual stumbling block.
362	
363	**Applying** a tag is a data-steward action, and on Snowflake it needs more than
364	the `CREATE TAG` grant that creates the tag object. Either:
365	
366	* `APPLY TAG` **on the account** — the global route; or
367	* `APPLY` on the **tag** *and* `OWNERSHIP` of the **object** being tagged.
368	
369	A role that can create the tag but does not own the table is refused. Verified
370	against a live warehouse, not inferred — though our run held both halves of the
371	second route at once (the steward created the tag and owned the table), so it
372	confirms the combination rather than isolating which half was doing the work.
373	
374	Related, if your connection uses one: a **role-scoped programmatic access token
375	cannot switch to another role**, even one the underlying user holds. A PAT issued
376	for a read-only role stays read-only no matter what the user is granted.
377	
378	**Reading** them needs nothing extra. DataQ queries
379	`INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TAG_REFERENCES_ALL_COLUMNS` (Snowflake) and
380	`information_schema.column_tags` (Unity Catalog) as the connection's own role —
381	no `ACCOUNT_USAGE` grant, no elevated identity. That is deliberate: `ACCOUNT_USAGE`
382	lags by up to two hours, and a *stale* classification is the failure this feature
383	exists to prevent.
384	
385	**That holds for `PRIVACY_CATEGORY` too**, which is worth stating because the tag
386	lives in the shared `SNOWFLAKE` database and a reasonable reader would expect it to
387	need `IMPORTED PRIVILEGES`. It does not: verified live against a connection role
388	holding no such grant, which nonetheless saw the tag and all three of its values.
389	The check mattered because failure here would be **silent** — a role that cannot
390	see a tag gets zero rows, not an error, so the column would look untagged and fall
391	back to the name heuristic. If you restrict tag visibility in your own account,
392	confirm your DataQ connection role can still read both tags.
393	
394	### Where it applies
395	
396	Only **Snowflake** and **Unity Catalog** have a column-tag concept. ADLS, S3,
397	Iceberg and flat files have no authoritative source to read, so for those the
398	classification remains the suite's own policy, the name/value classifier, and
399	fail-closed mode. This is a limit of the platforms, not a gap in the
400	implementation, and it is stated here so nobody plans around a guarantee that
401	cannot exist.
402	
403	### How fresh it is
404	
405	Tags are read **on each run** of a suite against that table and cached on the
406	asset. So a newly-classified column takes effect from the suite's next run —
407	including on samples captured *before* it was tagged, because a classification is
408	a statement about the data rather than about the moment it was read.
409	
410	If the tags cannot be read — no permission on the tag, a warehouse that is down —
411	DataQ logs it and behaves exactly as it did before the tag existed. It never
412	infers a clearance from a failed lookup, because a wrong guess in that direction
413	un-masks data.
414	
415	### Fail-closed mode
416	
417	For a dataset where "unclassified" should mean "do not show", set
418	`require_classification` on the suite's column policy. Nothing row-level is then
419	surfaced unless a column is explicitly cleared — by a `public`-family tag or by
420	your own `identifier_column`. The classifier is not consulted at all, which is the
421	point: a column called `field_7` full of national ID numbers looks harmless to a
422	name heuristic.
423	
424	It is off by default, and deliberately: a fully-masked failing row is
425	unactionable, so this is a trade you make for a regulated dataset rather than one
426	made for you.

428	## Data residency
429	
430	Where data lives, and what can take it elsewhere. GDPR Ch. V asks a controller to
431	answer both; this section describes **how DataQ answers them**, and
432	`GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` gives the answer for *your* instance, read live from
433	the running system (workspace-admin only) so it can be checked rather than
434	trusted.
435	
436	**One declared jurisdiction per deployment.** The unit that matters is the
437	*jurisdiction* — the country whose law applies — because that is what GDPR Ch. V
438	keys on; a cloud *region* is how a provider spells a location within one.
439	
440	The primary region is set by a single IaC variable (`azure_location` /
441	`aws_region`) and declared to the app as `DEPLOYMENT_REGION`. The app's value is a
442	**declaration, not a verification** — software cannot confirm which datacentre its
443	database sits in — and it is reported as `null` when unset, so an auditor sees a
444	gap rather than a guess.
445	
446	**This page deliberately does not state where any particular deployment sits.**
447	DataQ is customer-deployed: your regions are yours, they are set at deploy time,
448	and a region printed in a document is a snapshot that silently stops being true.
449	Read the live answer from the running instance instead —
450	`GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` (workspace-admin only) reports the declared region
451	and the enumerated transfer vectors from the system itself. A control you can
452	query beats a paragraph you have to trust.
453	
454	### Where each resource sits
455	
456	By default **every resource is in the declared region**, so the interesting rows
457	are the ones that cannot be:
458	
459	| Resource | Region | Holds customer data? |
460	|---|---|---|
461	| PostgreSQL, secret store, compute, object storage | the declared region | **Postgres holds the data** — suites, checks, results, and the incidental personal data in failing-row samples. The secret store holds warehouse credentials; compute holds data in transit only |
462	| Telemetry (App Insights / CloudWatch / OTLP) | the sink's region — **operator-chosen**, and may differ | Operational metadata; PII redacted at the logger |
463	| CloudFront (AWS only) | **global edge** | **No.** Only fingerprinted static assets are cached (`/assets/*.<ext>`); every other path is pass-through, so no API response and no failing-row sample is stored at an edge location |
464	| WAFv2 Web ACL (AWS only) | **`us-east-1`, unavoidably** | **No** — the ACL is rule configuration. CloudFront-scoped ACLs exist only in `us-east-1` regardless of where the stack lives |
465	
466	The CloudFront and WAF rows are stated rather than omitted so that a reviewer who
467	finds a `us-east-1` provider alias in an `eu-west` stack finds it explained here
468	rather than having to work out whether it matters. Both are properties of the
469	product, not of any one deployment.
470	
471	### When a resource legitimately sits elsewhere
472	
473	A deployment may attach the app to a **pre-existing** database server or Container
474	Apps environment — a subscription quota, or an organisation's shared-platform
475	policy, are the usual reasons. Its region was then fixed by whoever created it and
476	is not something this stack chooses.
477	
478	**The two are treated differently, on purpose.** A shared **database** in another
479	region is an **accepted exception rather than drift**: declare it with
480	`shared_pg_expected_location`, which turns "this server is somewhere else" from an
481	unexplained mismatch into a recorded decision.
482	
483	A shared **Container Apps environment** has **no such escape hatch, deliberately** —
484	it is compared against `azure_location` and a mismatch fails the plan outright. The
485	asymmetry follows from blast radius: one out-of-region database is a single
486	resource you can reason about, whereas the environment's region is inherited by
487	*every* Container App and Job in the stack, so accepting a mismatch there silently
488	relocates the entire deployment. Moving the app's compute to another jurisdiction
489	should require changing the declaration, not setting an override.
490	
491	The basis on which such an exception is acceptable is the part worth checking, and
492	it is **jurisdiction, not region**. Two regions inside one country engage no
493	Ch. V transfer. Two regions straddling an adequacy boundary do, whatever the
494	provider's console calls them — so an operator in a regime that cares about
495	sub-national placement, or one deploying across an EU boundary, must consolidate
496	rather than inherit somebody else's reasoning.
497	
498	### The assertions that catch drift
499	
500	The Azure stack can share a Container Apps environment, declared as a `data`
501	source — so its region is set by whoever created it, and **every Container App and
502	Job in the stack inherits it** (a Job must sit in its environment's region). Left
503	unchecked, moving or recreating that shared environment elsewhere would relocate
504	all of the app's compute with a clean `apply` and no signal.
505	
506	`aca.tf` therefore carries a `postcondition` comparing the shared environment's
507	actual location against `var.azure_location`, so a mismatch **fails the plan**
508	with a message naming both. For a Ch. V control, "we did not notice the
509	jurisdiction changed" is the whole failure mode.
510	
511	A shared **database** gets the same comparison as a `check` block, which **warns**
512	rather than blocking. A `postcondition` there would fail every apply until someone
513	migrated a database, and the right response to "the DB moved" is a decision, not a
514	rollback.
515	
516	It compares against `shared_pg_expected_location`, which **defaults to
517	`azure_location`** — so for an ordinary single-region deployment the two are the
518	same thing and the check is silent. Setting the variable is how a deployment
519	records an accepted exception. That indirection is the difference between a check
520	that still works and one that warns on every plan forever: an accepted exception
521	must not cost you the detector, and it must not hand the noise to every other
522	deployment either.
523	
524	**One drafting lesson, kept because it argues for the paragraph above.** An
525	earlier version of this page tabulated a specific deployment's regions. One row
526	asserted the database sat in the declared region; checking the running deployment
527	showed it did not, and had not for some time. Nobody had lied — the document had
528	simply been written once and the infrastructure had moved. That is the failure
529	mode of publishing per-deployment facts, and it is why this page now describes the
530	mechanism and points you at the live endpoint for the values.
531	
532	### What can move data out
533	
534	Enumerated at `GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` — enumerated rather than derived, so
535	a vector that is switched **off** still appears and an auditor can see it was
536	considered:
537	
538	- **Alert delivery** — webhooks and email carry check names, statuses and, when a
539	  failing sample is included, *redacted* sample values. The destination is
540	  operator-configured and its location is outside DataQ's knowledge.
541	- **Telemetry** — traces and logs to an operator-chosen sink; PII is redacted at
542	  the logger, so this is operational metadata rather than warehouse values.
543	- **MCP AI clients** — **live today.** `/mcp` serves run results, redacted failing
544	  samples and check configuration to whatever AI client holds a valid PAT. The
545	  model provider behind that client, and its jurisdiction, are chosen by the token
546	  holder and are outside DataQ's knowledge. This is the more consequential of the
547	  two LLM entries, and an earlier draft listed only the other one.
548	- **LLM intelligence** — the *outbound* direction, DataQ calling a model on its
549	  own behalf: **built, off by default** until an admin configures a provider and
550	  credential, sent to that admin-chosen endpoint. SQL-generation and
551	  check-suggestion prompts are schema plus masked aggregate profiler statistics;
552	  root-cause-analysis narratives additionally send the triggering check's own
553	  observed value — routed through the same column-policy/warehouse-tag floor
554	  every other results surface applies — and its expected value (a
555	  check-authored threshold, not warehouse data, so never masked). **Never raw
556	  sample rows**, on either path. Every call — feature invocation or admin test
557	  probe alike — is recorded with requester and token counts.
558	- **Sign-in email** — email-OTP codes to user addresses via the configured SMTP
559	  relay: account identifiers rather than warehouse content, relay operator-chosen.
560	- **Secret store** — warehouse credentials in Key Vault / Secrets Manager /
561	  OpenBao. Not customer data, but a remote store is a location, and the
562	  credentials it holds unlock the systems the customer data lives in.
563	
564	Deploying into another jurisdiction is a variable change, not a fork: the same
565	images and the same IaC take a different region. What DataQ does **not** do is
566	verify the result — that remains the deploying organization's attestation, which
567	is the correct split for a customer-deployed product.
568	
569	## Compliance — GDPR / CCPA-CPRA / HIPAA
570	
571	**What this is:** a summary of how the technical controls above map onto the major
572	data-protection regimes. **What this is not:** a legal compliance certification. Much of
573	GDPR/HIPAA is *organizational* (DPAs, BAAs, DPIAs, consent, lawful basis, breach process)
574	and is the deploying organization's responsibility, not the codebase's.
575	
576	### Roles & deployment model
577	
578	DataQ ships as **customer-deployed, bring-your-own-license** software, not multi-tenant
579	hosted SaaS. That fixes the data-protection role split:
580	
581	- **The deploying organization is the data *controller*** (GDPR) / *covered entity* or
582	  *business* (HIPAA / CCPA). It chooses the region, owns the warehouse data, holds any LLM
583	  credential, and carries consent / lawful-basis / DPA / BAA obligations.
584	- **DataQ (the software) is a *processor* / *business associate*.** Its job is to provide
585	  the technical controls — security of processing, minimization, deletion levers,
586	  auditability — the controller needs to *be* compliant.
587	
588	We do not market "DataQ is GDPR/HIPAA compliant" — no software can be. The honest claim is
589	**processor-grade technical controls for GDPR / CCPA / HIPAA workloads**: an access audit
590	trail, data-subject-rights tooling, authoritative PII/PHI classification, a declared and
591	enforced deployment region, and encryption at rest — each covered in its own section above.
592	
593	Personal data / PHI appears only *incidentally* in DataQ — in failing-row samples and, for
594	a set-oriented expectation's full observed-value list, in a result's `observed_value`. There
595	is no core people-database; HIPAA applies only when a customer points DataQ at PHI, GDPR
596	only to EU personal data.
597	
598	### Per-regulation summary
599	
600	| Regulation | Applies when | Controls in place |
601	|---|---|---|
602	| **GDPR** | EU personal data in scope | Privacy-by-design handling (logger-level redaction, retention limits); access audit trail ([Authentication & access](#authentication-access)); data-subject-rights export/erasure (below); declared + enforced residency ([Data residency](#data-residency)) |
603	| **CCPA / CPRA** | CA residents' data, "business" threshold | No sale of data; deletion via retention purge + the data-subject-rights erasure lever below; right-to-know via the export lever |
604	| **HIPAA** | Customer processes **PHI** | Encryption in transit/at rest ([Encryption](#encryption)); access control (roles + suite grants); audit controls — config changes *and* data reads recorded, admin-queryable, and hash-chained for tamper-evidence (unanchored to an external log sink by default); a BAA remains the deploying organization's obligation |
605	
606	### Data-subject rights (export / erasure)
607	
608	DataQ has no people-table of its own, so a subject is identified the same way the
609	controller's own warehouse identifies them: an Admin-only `(column, value)` workflow.
610	`POST /api/v1/admin/data-subject-requests/export` returns every matching failing-row-sample
611	cell **unredacted** (the access/portability right) across every suite in the workspace, and
612	records an access-audit event. The erasure counterpart removes only the matching row/cell —
613	the rest of a result's captured sample survives. Both run synchronously and are recorded in
614	the audit trail. Full mechanism and a verification walkthrough are in the
615	[data-subject-rights runbook](compliance/data-subject-rights-runbook.md). The controller's
616	own warehouse remains their own responsibility — this covers only what DataQ itself has
617	captured.
618	
619	### Audit-log tamper-evidence
620	
621	The `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE` on `audit_events` ([Authentication & access](#authentication-access))
622	guards against **accidental** in-app mutation only — the table's owner can grant the
623	privileges back, and the retention sweep does exactly that, by necessity. Every event is
624	additionally **hash-chained** to the one before it: `GET /admin/audit-events/verify`
625	(workspace-admin gated) recomputes the chain and reports the first break, and a daily
626	scheduled task runs the same check unattended. Retention purges checkpoint the boundary
627	they create before deleting, so a documented purge reads as clean rather than as tampering.
628	
629	**The chain alone is not the tamper-evidence claim — an external anchor is.** An actor with
630	write access to the *whole* table could recompute the chain forward from wherever they
631	edited, proving nothing to that specific adversary. An optional `TamperAnchor` publishes the
632	chain head, HMAC-signed, to an operator-controlled endpoint outside the database (a webhook
633	to a separate log sink or append-only object store) — DataQ never reads it back, which is
634	the whole point. It is **off by default**; an operator whose regime requires a provably
635	unaltered log must configure it.
636	
637	### Organizational artifacts
638	
639	Templates and reference documents for the parts of compliance that are genuinely
640	organizational, published alongside this page:

642	- [Sub-processor / third-party disclosure](compliance/sub-processors.md) — every external
643	  service the software can send data to.
644	- [DPIA input sheet](compliance/dpia-input-sheet.md) — the personal-data inventory only the
645	  software can supply: data classes, per-location retention, and controls.
646	- [Breach-notification runbook](compliance/breach-notification-runbook.md) — a
647	  reference-deployment procedure plus a template for customer deployments.
648	- [DPA / BAA templates](compliance/dpa-baa-templates.md) — drafted with accurate technical
649	  annexes and marked **counsel-review-required**; not an engineering sign-off.
650	  Consent/lawful-basis guidance stays with the deploying organization.

653

_PIPELINE_HISTORY_LIMIT = 10

_SAME_ASSET_SIBLING_WINDOW = timedelta(days=7)
_SAME_ASSET_SIBLING_LIMIT = 20

# values (vs. the scalar `unexpected_count`/`unexpected_percent` aggregates).
_SAMPLE_LIST_KEYS = frozenset({"partial_unexpected_list", "unexpected_index_list"})

#: modules (e.g. `llm_rca`) import rather than re-spelling this set independently (#1633 review).

def _layer(name: str, fn: Callable[[], Any]) -> Any:
    """Run one evidence layer best-effort: any failure logs a structured warning
    and degrades that layer to ``None`` — never poisoning the card (and through
    it the whole run's incident sync).
    """
    try:
        return fn()
    except Exception:
        log.warning("incident_evidence_layer_failed", layer=name)
        return None


def _num(value: Decimal | None) -> float | None:
    """Widen a NUMERIC metric to a JSON-friendly float (``None`` stays ``None``)."""
    return float(value) if value is not None else None


def _iso(value: datetime | None) -> str | None:
    return value.isoformat() if value is not None else None


def build_evidence(
    session: Session,
    *,
    run: Run,
    result: Result,
    check: Check | None,
    asset: Asset | None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Assemble the layer-1 evidence card for a breaching ``result`` on ``run``."""
    now = datetime.now(UTC)
    return {
        "generated_at": now.isoformat(),
        "check": _layer("check", lambda: _check_layer(check)),
        "asset": _layer("asset", lambda: _asset_layer(asset)),
        "failing_result": _layer(
            "failing_result",
            lambda: _failing_result_layer(
                session, run=run, result=result, check=check, asset=asset
            ),
        ),
        "kind_detail": _layer("kind_detail", lambda: _kind_detail_layer(check, result)),
        "metric_trend": _layer(
            "metric_trend", lambda: _metric_trend_layer(session, check_id=result.check_id)
        ),
        "sibling_checks": _layer(
            "sibling_checks",
            lambda: _sibling_checks_layer(session, run=run, exclude_check_id=result.check_id),
        ),
        "same_asset_siblings": _layer(
            "same_asset_siblings",
            lambda: _same_asset_siblings_layer(
                session, asset=asset, exclude_check_id=result.check_id, now=now
            ),
        ),
        "upstream_pipeline_run": _layer(
            "upstream_pipeline_run", lambda: _upstream_pipeline_layer(session, run=run)
        ),
        "downstream_blast_radius": _layer(
            "downstream_blast_radius", lambda: _blast_radius_layer(session, asset=asset)
        ),
        # Needs a live datasource profile of both batches — not existing data, not
        # cheap. Documented null placeholder (see module docstring).
        "profile_diff": None,
    }


def _check_layer(check: Check | None) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    if check is None:
        return None
    return {
        "id": str(check.id),
        "name": check.name,
        "expectation_type": check.expectation_type,
        "kind": check.kind,
    }


def _asset_layer(asset: Asset | None) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    if asset is None:
        return None
    return {
        "id": str(asset.id),
        "namespace": asset.namespace,
        "name": asset.name,
        "env": asset.env,
    }


def _failing_result_layer(
    session: Session, *, run: Run, result: Result, check: Check | None, asset: Asset | None
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """The breaching result — status + metric + GX aggregates. **No sample rows.**
    ``sample_failures`` is never read.

    ``observed_value`` can itself carry a literal warehouse cell value (or a
    list of them) for an expectation-kind check's min/max/mean-style rules —
    real target data, not just GX metadata. This card is built ONCE here and
    stored on the `Incident` row (workspace-true, like `same_asset_siblings`

    """
    observed = _strip_sample_lists(result.observed_value)
    if check is not None:

            tested_column=tested_column,
            policy=suite.column_policy if suite is not None else None,
            tags=tags,

    return {
        "status": result.status,
        "metric_value": _num(result.metric_value),
        "observed_value": observed,
        "expected_value": result.expected_value,
    }


def _strip_sample_lists(observed: dict[str, Any] | None) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    """Drop the list-valued sample-bearing keys from an ``observed_value`` dict
    (see ``_SAMPLE_LIST_KEYS``); non-dict / ``None`` shapes pass through.
    """
    if not isinstance(observed, dict):
        return observed
    return {key: val for key, val in observed.items() if key not in _SAMPLE_LIST_KEYS}

1	# The incident evidence card
2	
3	When a check breaches into a warning or failure severe enough to open or update an incident,
4	DataQ assembles a fixed, deterministic snapshot of everything relevant to that failure —
5	**before** any narrative is generated over it, not as part of generating one. This page is that
6	snapshot's contract: what each layer contains, what it is computed from, what a `null` in it
7	actually means, and the privacy guarantee it carries.
8	
9	The card is deterministic on purpose. A narrative generated later (see
10	[MCP tool design: honesty & disclosure](mcp-honesty.md) for the same discipline applied to the
11	rest of the AI-facing surface) can only ever reason over this fixed bundle — it never goes back
12	to a live datasource, and every claim it makes must cite which layer below supports it. The
13	evidence is gathered the same way regardless of whether any narrative is ever requested over it.
14	
15	## What it is a snapshot of
16	
17	The card is captured at the moment an incident opens or re-occurs — it describes **that
18	occurrence**, not the current live state of the check, the asset, or the pipeline. A check
19	renamed since, or a table that has since recovered, still reads through the card as it was at
20	the time of the breach. Read it as "when this last failed," never as "right now."
21	
22	## The layers
23	
24	| Layer | Contains | Computed from |
25	|---|---|---|
26	| `check` | The failing check's id, name, expectation type, and monitor kind | The check row at capture time |
27	| `asset` | The table/file this check runs against | The resolved asset for the run |
28	| `failing_result` | Status, the numeric metric, the GX-shaped observed/expected values | The breaching result — **no failing sample rows**, see below |
29	| `kind_detail` | The kind-specific fields (e.g. `age_hours` for freshness, `z_score` for anomaly) pulled out of the raw result, so a reader doesn't need to know all four monitor-kind JSON shapes | `failing_result`'s own observed value, reshaped |
30	| `metric_trend` | The 10 most recent readings for this check, newest first | This check's own result history |
31	| `sibling_checks` | Every other check's outcome in the **same run** | The run the failing result belongs to |
32	| `same_asset_siblings` | The latest outcome of every *other* check targeting this **same asset**, across every suite, from the last 7 days | Every suite's results on this asset, not just this run's |
33	| `upstream_pipeline_run` | The orchestration pipeline run that triggered this suite run, its duration, and its delay against that pipeline's own recent history | The linked `pipeline_runs` row, when one triggered this run |
34	| `downstream_blast_radius` | The assets reachable downstream of this one via recorded lineage | The lineage graph, depth-capped |
35	| `profile_diff` | Always `null` | Not implemented — see below |
36	
37	## The privacy guarantee
38	
39	`failing_result` never carries a failing sample row — the specific record values that tripped
40	the check are deliberately excluded from the card at the point it is built, not filtered out
41	later. A narrative generated over this card, or a client reading it directly, can describe *that
42	a column failed a null check* but cannot see *which row*. Use the run's own results — which
43	apply the product's standard column-aware redaction — to inspect specific failing values.
44	
45	`same_asset_siblings` is assembled once, for the workspace as a whole, with no caller in scope —
46	it has to be, since it draws from every suite that touches the asset, not just the one that
47	opened this incident. Reading it back applies a second, per-request narrowing: a caller only
48	sees the sibling entries on suites they hold at least view access to; entries from suites they
49	cannot see are withheld and folded into a count instead of being named. An outbound alert
50	narrows the same layer differently — to entries on the incident's own suite only, since an alert
51	channel has no per-viewer grant to check it against.
52	
53	## Reading a `null` layer correctly
54	
55	A `null` layer does not by itself mean something went wrong — each layer means a different thing
56	by it, and collapsing them into one "missing data" reading is the mistake this section exists to
57	prevent:
58	
59	- **`upstream_pipeline_run` is `null` for the ordinary case** — a manually-triggered or
60	  scheduled run, which is most runs. It means no orchestration pipeline triggered this run, not
61	  that one should have and didn't.
62	- **`kind_detail` is `null` for an ordinary expectation or comparison check** — the common case,
63	  where the result's own observed value already is the shape a reader wants, so there is nothing
64	  to lift out. For a freshness, volume, schema-drift, or anomaly check, by contrast, the card is
65	  only ever captured from a genuinely warned, failed, or critical occurrence — never an
66	  operational error or a skip — so a `null` there for one of those four kinds means the same rare
67	  thing a missing `check` layer means: the check itself is gone.
68	- **`metric_trend`, `sibling_checks`, and `same_asset_siblings` are `[]`, not `null`, when there
69	  is genuinely nothing to show.** A `null` in one of these three specifically means the layer
70	  could not be built at all (an unexpected failure while assembling it) — distinct from an empty
71	  result, which means it was built successfully and found nothing.
72	- **`downstream_blast_radius` being `[]` has three different real causes that read identically**:
73	  the asset could not be resolved, the asset is a genuine lineage leaf, or the workspace has no
74	  lineage recorded at all. An empty list here is a floor, not proof that nothing is affected
75	  downstream.
76	- **`profile_diff` is always `null`.** This is a documented placeholder for a comparison DataQ
77	  does not yet compute (it would need a live datasource read of both the before and after batch,
78	  not just already-captured data) — not a failed attempt, and not specific to any one incident.
79	
80	## The provenance rule a narrative inherits
81	
82	When a narrative is generated over this card, every claim it makes must cite which of a closed,
83	fixed set of layer names it rests on: `failing_result`, `kind_detail`, `metric_trend`,
84	`sibling_checks`, `same_asset_siblings`, `upstream_pipeline_run`, `downstream_blast_radius`, and
85	`check_history` — a longer per-check result history fetched alongside the card, not one of the
86	card's own fields, since the card itself keeps only the last 10 points. `check`, `asset`, and the
87	always-null `profile_diff` are identifying context, not evidence a hypothesis can be pinned to,
88	so they are deliberately outside this set. A hypothesis that cannot point to a real layer in it
89	is refused before it can ever reach a reader. The generation step also computes, deterministically and
90	without ever asking the model, what the snapshot could not see — a withheld cross-suite sibling
91	count, an unresolved upstream pipeline, no recorded downstream lineage — because a model cannot
92	be trusted to notice or disclose a gap it was never shown existed in the first place.

1	# DPIA input sheet — what personal data DataQ can hold
2	
3	> **Who this is for:** a controller running a Data Protection Impact Assessment
4	> (GDPR Art 35) or a HIPAA risk analysis over a deployment of DataQ. This sheet is
5	> the processor-side input **only DataQ can supply**: the complete inventory of
6	> personal data the software can hold, where each item lives, how long it is kept,
7	> and which controls apply. Everything here describes the software's mechanisms;
8	> your deployment's concrete regions and endpoints are readable from
9	> `GET /api/v1/admin/deployment`, per the [residency posture](../security.md#data-residency).
10	
11	## The framing that bounds the assessment
12	
13	DataQ is a data-quality tool, not a people database. Personal data appears in two
14	distinct classes:
15	
16	1. **Incidental warehouse data** — values copied out of *your* monitored tables
17	   when a check fails. DataQ never ingests tables wholesale; it stores small
18	   evidence samples of failing rows. Whether those contain personal data depends
19	   entirely on what you point it at.
20	2. **Workspace account data** — the identities of the people who use DataQ
21	   itself: emails, display names, roles, sign-in state.
22	
23	The controller's warehouse remains the controller's responsibility — DataQ reads
24	it but is not its system of record.
25	
26	## Class 1 — incidental warehouse data
27	
28	| Where | What | Retention | Controls |
29	|---|---|---|---|
30	| `results.sample_failures` | Up to a bounded number of failing rows per check result, as column→value maps | `SAMPLE_FAILURES_RETENTION_DAYS` (default **30**); daily purge sets the column NULL and stamps `sample_failures_purged_at` — the row and its `metric_value` trend survive, the personal data does not | Column-aware **redaction ladder** on every read surface (REST, MCP, alert delivery), driven by the per-suite column policy, the governance floor from warehouse-native PII tags (G3, `services/column_tags.py`), and fail-closed mode (`require_classification`) |
31	| `results.observed_value` (list-shaped) | A set-oriented expectation's full observed distinct-value list can reproduce column values | Same purge as `sample_failures` | Same redaction ladder |
32	| `results.observed_value` (scalar `unparsed_value` cell) | A single unparseable cell value captured for diagnosis | `SAMPLE_FAILURES_RETENTION_DAYS`, same purge as the two rows above | Redaction ladder applies on read |
33	| Dry-run / live-probe responses | Real values shown to the check author; **nothing persisted** | Not stored (structurally cannot persist) | Fail-closed suites mask even here; REST dry-run values are shown unredacted by design, a recorded decision |
34	
35	**Erasure status — state it honestly in your DPIA:** deletion happens on the
36	retention clock and via entity cascade (deleting a suite/check destroys its
37	results) **and, on demand, via the [data-subject-rights runbook](data-subject-rights-runbook.md)** — an
38	Admin-only capability that identifies a subject by a `(column, value)` pair (the
39	same key the controller's own warehouse row uses; DataQ has no people-table) and
40	surgically removes only the matching row/cell from `sample_failures` /
41	`observed_value`, leaving the rest of a result's captured sample — other rows,
42	other subjects — intact.
43	
44	## Class 2 — workspace account data
45	
46	| Where | What | Retention | Controls |
47	|---|---|---|---|
48	| `users` | Email (unique, lower-cased), display name, OIDC subject id + issuer, workspace role | Life of the account | Role-gated admin surface; ADR 0033 two-axis authz |
49	| `sessions` | OTP-mode sign-in sessions — **token hash only** (never the token) | Server-side revocation; logout deletes | HttpOnly cookie; SHA-256 at rest |
50	| `otp_codes` | One-time codes — **hashed**, attempt-capped | Expired codes purged daily (`purge_otp_codes` beat) | Rate limits + enumeration-resistant responses |
51	| `api_keys` | PATs — **SHA-256 hash only**, name, last-used | Until revoked | `dq_live_` prefix supports secret scanning |
52	| `audit_events` | Actor email/id, action, target — the append-only audit trail (ADR 0041) | `AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS` (default **365**), independent of the sample purge — one clock keeps a record, the other destroys one | Append-only (`REVOKE UPDATE/DELETE`); **no warehouse values ever copied in** (ADR 0041 §2.6) — read events name *which* result was read, never what it contained. Hash-chained for tamper-evidence, unanchored to an external log sink by default |
53	| Logs / telemetry | Request ids, structured events | Sink-controlled | **PII redacted at the logger level** — the redactor sits in `core/logging.py`, so a dependency's log line is scrubbed too |
54	
55	## The rows a DPIA form usually asks for
56	
57	| DPIA question | DataQ answer |
58	|---|---|
59	| Lawful-basis notes | DataQ is a **processor** (BYOL, ADR 0013); the deploying controller holds lawful basis for the warehouse data it monitors. Workspace accounts: legitimate interest / contract (employee tooling). |
60	| Data subjects | Whoever appears in monitored tables (controller-determined); workspace users (employees/contractors of the controller). |
61	| Special categories | Only if the controller points checks at such columns. Mitigations: column policy + warehouse-native tag floor (G3) + fail-closed mode for suites that must never show values. |
62	| Cross-border transfers | Enumerated, not derived — see the [sub-processor disclosure](sub-processors.md) and the residency posture. The outbound-LLM vector is **built, off by default** — live only once an admin configures a provider and credential. SQL-generation and check-suggestion prompts use masked aggregate profiler statistics; RCA narratives additionally send the triggering check's own observed value, masked through that same column-policy/warehouse-tag floor, and its expected value (a check-authored threshold, not warehouse data). Never raw sample rows on either path. MCP clients are the token-holder's choice. |
63	| Access ("who saw it") | G1 read events: data reads on REST **and** MCP are recorded and admin-queryable. |
64	| Erasure ("how is it removed") | Retention purge (30-day default) + entity cascade, **and** on-demand targeted erasure by `(column, value)` — the [data-subject-rights runbook](data-subject-rights-runbook.md). |
65	| Security of processing | See [Security & data handling](../security.md): secrets in a dedicated store, TLS, rate limiting, security headers, single public surface, non-root containers, least-privilege DB role. |

1	# Third-party services & sub-processor disclosure
2	
3	> **Who this is for:** the organization deploying DataQ (the data **controller** /
4	> covered entity) and its privacy/security reviewers. DataQ ships as
5	> **customer-deployed BYOL** (ADR 0013): there is no DataQ-hosted SaaS, so DataQ
6	> the company holds none of your data and, in the classic GDPR Art 28 sense, has
7	> **no sub-processors of your data at all**. What a controller still needs from us —
8	> and cannot produce themselves — is the list below: **every external service the
9	> software can send data to**, so your own sub-processor register and DPIA can
10	> name them. Which entries apply to *your* deployment depends on what you enable
11	> and where you point it.
12	
13	## How to read this list
14	
15	Every row is a **capability of the software**, enumerated whether or not it is
16	enabled — the same enumerate-don't-derive rule as the
17	[residency posture](../security.md#data-residency), so a reviewer can see a vector
18	was considered rather than inferring its absence. For the live state of *your*
19	deployment, query `GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` (workspace-admin only), which
20	reports the enabled transfer vectors without shell access.
21	
22	The **operator column is you**: in every row, the receiving service is chosen,
23	contracted, and configured by the deploying organization. DataQ never defaults to
24	a third-party endpoint.
25	
26	## The vectors
27	
28	| # | Service (operator-chosen) | What DataQ sends | Personal data? | When active |
29	|---|---|---|---|---|
30	| 1 | **Monitored datasources** — Snowflake, ADLS Gen2, S3 / S3-compatible, Unity Catalog, Iceberg | Read-only queries; DQ check SQL | Reads whatever the monitored tables hold — this is the primary data flow | Always (the product's purpose) |
31	| 2 | **Orchestration providers** — ADF, Airflow, dbt | Polling reads of pipeline/DAG run status; inbound webhooks | No — pipeline metadata only | When orchestration connections exist |
32	| 3 | **Alert delivery** — MS Teams / Slack webhooks, SMTP email (incl. SES) | Check names, statuses, suite names and — when a failing sample is attached — **redacted** sample values | Potentially, in redacted failing samples; recipient addresses | When notifications are configured |
33	| 4 | **Sign-in email (OTP)** — the configured SMTP relay | One-time codes to user email addresses | User email addresses (account identifiers, not warehouse content) | `otp` auth mode |
34	| 5 | **OIDC identity provider** — Azure AD, AWS Cognito, any standards-compliant issuer | Standard OIDC flows; DataQ receives (never sends) profile claims | User identity (email, name, subject id) held at the IdP | `oidc` auth mode |
35	| 6 | **Secret store** — Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, OpenBao/Vault | Warehouse credentials (write on connection create, read at run time) | No customer data — but the credentials unlock the systems that hold it | Always (one of the four backends) |
36	| 7 | **Telemetry** — Azure Application Insights, AWS X-Ray/CloudWatch, any OTLP sink | Traces + structured logs, **PII-redacted at the logger** | Operational metadata; request ids, not warehouse values | When an exporter is configured |
37	| 8 | **MCP AI clients** — whatever model provider stands behind a client holding a valid PAT | Run results, redacted failing samples, check configuration, via the 46 `/mcp` tools | Potentially, in redacted samples — the model provider and its jurisdiction are **chosen by the token holder** | When PATs are issued and `/mcp` is reachable |
38	| 9 | **Outbound LLM intelligence** — DataQ calling a model on its own behalf | Schema + masked profiler statistics for SQL generation and check suggestions; RCA narratives additionally send the triggering check's own observed value, routed through that same column-policy/warehouse-tag masking floor, and its expected value (a check-authored threshold, not warehouse data, so never masked). Never raw sample rows | Potentially — profiler statistics or an observed value, both subject to the masking floor; model provider and jurisdiction are admin-chosen | **Live, off by default** — an admin must configure a provider + credential before any call leaves |
39	| 10 | **Lineage provider** — Marquez / OpenLineage-compatible catalog | Pull of lineage graph metadata | No — table/job names, not row data | When `LINEAGE_PROVIDER` is configured |
40	
41	Cloud-platform services that *host* a deployment (the managed Postgres, Redis,
42	container runtime, object storage of your chosen cloud) are your cloud provider
43	acting as **your** processor under your existing cloud agreement — they are in
44	scope for your register but are not DataQ-specific and are not repeated here.
45	
46	## Keeping this current — the process
47	
48	This list changes only when the software's outbound surface changes, so it is
49	maintained as code review discipline, not a calendar:
50	
51	1. **Any PR that adds an outbound network call to a new service class must update
52	   this page in the same PR** — same rule as the residency enumeration.
53	2. The **quarterly supply-chain audit** (CONTRIBUTING rule 39) re-checks the list

55	3. The **LLM row flips from "not built"** in the PR that ships the intelligence
56	   feature — that PR is the Ch. V trigger the DPIA sheet also names.
